3	description: Read and act on the Archon Horizon inbox — list/filter items, understand labels/kinds, comment, archive, create; per-team ownership and read-state; and message other projects or teams via the `horizon inbox` CLI.
4	---
5	
6	The inbox is the durable channel between the human, agent sessions (present and
7	future), and other projects. Act on it through the CLI; never edit inbox files
8	by hand. Prefer `--json` whenever reading command output for exact ids or
9	fields.
10	
11	## Read
12	
13	- `horizon inbox list` — read the inbox. Use `--json` when you need exact ids,
14	  labels, scope, author, audience, timestamps, or comments. Use the list filters
15	  to narrow without losing the overview: `--to horizon`, `--to human`,
16	  `--project P`, repeated `--kind K`, repeated `--label L`,
17	  `--status open`, `--query TEXT`, `--limit N`, and `--comments N`.
18	- In an agent session, an unqualified list means the **open working queue**, not
19	  archived history. It is ordered by attention: required protections first,
20	  unread/direct conversations next, then advisory items. JSON starts with an
21	  `attention` summary so redirecting stderr cannot erase this signal.
22	- `horizon inbox show <id> --json` opens exactly one item and marks it read for
23	  your team. Use `--no-mark-read` for inspection without acknowledgement.
24	- Every inbox command evaluates the full local working set, even when `list` is
25	  filtered. Treat its advisory warnings as a prompt to review duplicates, stale
26	  memories, and consumed notices. The CLI never archives automatically because
27	  only the working agent can decide what is resolved; that agent must make an
28	  explicit cleanup pass before its final report.
29	- Labels are the release gate. Local inbox items default to `agent-ready`, which
30	  means they are visible to agents at run boundaries. Keep that default for
31	  machine-addressed work, and usually keep it for human-addressed notices too:
32	  it helps later agents see that the human has already been notified and avoids
33	  duplicate reports. Use `not-ready`, `rejected`, or no labels only when there is
34	  a concrete reason agents should not see or act on the item yet.
35	- Audience says who should read the item: empty/general, `horizon`, `human`,
36	  `project:<name>`, or a **direct message** to another team: `task:<id>` /
37	  `run:<id>` (older items may carry the legacy `ground` audience). A conversation
38	  may have several recipients; start one with `horizon inbox dm <recipient>...`.
39	  Scope/project says what the item is about.
40	- Horizon reads general items, items addressed to `horizon`, items addressed
41	  to its project, and DMs addressed to its own task/run. It should ignore other
42	  projects' and other teams' addressed items.
43	- A conversation's participants are its recipients **and its initiator**. The
44	  initiator is recorded as `metadata.started_by`; replies become unread for every
45	  other participant, including that initiator. Participants are not ownership:
46	  the initiator remains responsible for deciding when the thread is finished.
47	- Kinds: `conversation` (a direct/group thread requiring prompt acknowledgement),
48	  `hint` (normal guidance), `issue` (problem to fix/report),
49	  `protection` (standing constraint / soft freeze), `info` (a notice for the
50	  human — something you did or noticed they should know, e.g. a renamed project
51	  or an important change; purely informational, never affects what runs),
52	  `memory` (durable agent note or dead end).
53	
54	## Ownership & read-state (your team's inbox)
55	
56	Each running session is a **team**, and the inbox is shared across teams. Two
57	lightweight overlays keep it navigable:
58	
59	- **Ownership** — an item is either *shared with everyone* (the default) or
60	  *owned by one task* (that team's private inbox — e.g. its own memory). Read your
61	  team's inbox with `horizon inbox list --mine` (owned-by-you **plus** shared);
62	  another team's private items don't appear. Own an item to your task with
63	  `horizon inbox add --mine …` (or `--owner <task-id>`), and `horizon inbox own
64	  <id> --mine|--owner <task>|--shared` to move an existing one. Owning your
65	  `--kind memory` notes keeps another team's memory out of your working set.
66	- **Read-state** — read/unread is **per team**, so a shared item several teams see
67	  tracks who has read it. `horizon inbox list --unread` is what *you* have not read
68	  yet; `horizon inbox read <id>` marks it read, and `horizon inbox unread <id>`
69	  puts it back (e.g. you read it but it still needs action). Combine:
70	  `horizon inbox list --mine --unread` is your team's fresh queue — the same signal
71	  the pre-command synchronizer counts for you.
72	
73	Read in this order before editing:
74	
75	1. `horizon inbox list --mine --status open --kind protection --json` — every
76	   active protection is required even if your team previously marked it read.
77	2. `horizon inbox list --mine --unread --kind conversation --json` — open each
78	   result with `inbox show`; reply when a response is needed, otherwise the read
79	   acknowledgement clears it until another participant replies.
80	3. Consult hint/issue/info/memory items as advisory context for the task.
81	
82	The reader/owner id is inferred from your session (your task), so you rarely pass
83	it explicitly.
84	
85	## Act
86	
87	Authorship is automatic: every item and comment you create through the CLI is
88	attributed to your role (normally `horizon`) from the run environment — you do
89	**not** pass `--author` (a stray `--author work-reviewer` is demoted to the
90	`agent` metadata, not used as the author, so the author set stays conventional).
91	If you are a dispatched **subagent**, add `--agent <your-name>` (e.g. `--agent
92	work-reviewer`) to record your identity; it is stored in metadata and shown
93	next to the role in the UI, keeping the author itself a clean role. Items and
94	comments are also auto-tagged with the run/session provenance (a small chip in the
95	UI); you do not pass this yourself.
96	
97	New inbox items use a two-part body:
98	
99	- First paragraph = concise title. Keep it short enough to scan in one UI row
100	  (aim for under ~100 characters); do not put the full explanation here.
101	- Second paragraph and later = non-empty description. Put the evidence, impact,
102	  next action, and relevant ids/files here. The description is **mandatory** — an
103	  item that is only a title is rejected.
104	
105	Write bodies and comments in **Markdown**: the dashboard renders it. Use short
106	paragraphs and `-` bullet lists instead of one wall-of-text paragraph, `**bold**`
107	for the key claim, and backticks for ids, lemma names, files, and code
108	(`` `lem:foo` ``, `` `Foo.lean:42` ``). For a multi-part result, start with a
109	one-sentence conclusion, then use `## Result`, `## Evidence`, `## Impact`, and
110	`## Next action` as applicable; omit empty sections. The CLI rejects long new
111	agent descriptions, opening messages, and comments with no paragraph, heading,
112	or list structure.
113	
114	Do not create an item whose body is only a title. If you need a `[persistent]` or
115	`[temporary]` tag, put it at the start of the title paragraph and keep the rest
116	of that paragraph concise.
117	
118	Before opening a new item, search the open inbox for the same topic using
119	`horizon inbox list --status open --query "key words" --json` and, when relevant,
120	`--project P` / `--to R`. If a live item already covers the same issue, do not
121	open a duplicate: add a comment with the new evidence, or edit the body if the
122	main description is stale. If you discover an open item is obsolete, already
123	solved, consumed, or superseded, add a short comment when the reason is not
124	obvious and then run `horizon inbox archive <id>`.
125	
126	### Conversation lifecycle
127	
128	A conversation is for an expected reply, decision, or active coordination. A
129	one-way handoff or announcement is an `info`/`hint`, not a conversation.
130	
131	1. **Search before starting:** inspect open conversations for the same topic and
132	   participants (`inbox list --status open --kind conversation --query "key words"
133	   --json`). Reply to the existing thread whenever it can carry the update. Do not
134	   open one thread per incremental finding.
135	2. **One question, one thread:** keep follow-ups, answers, corrections, and the
136	   final decision as comments on that thread. Start another only when it has a
137	   genuinely different decision boundary or participant set.
138	3. **Answer before branching:** when a conversation becomes unread, open it and
139	   answer or acknowledge it before starting another conversation with the same
140	   team.
141	4. **The initiator closes:** if `metadata.started_by` is your task/run, you own
142	   the lifecycle. Once the requested answer has arrived and been consumed, add a
143	   short conclusion comment when the outcome is not obvious, then
144	   `horizon inbox archive <id>`. Do this during the session, not only after a
145	   warning says the inbox is full.
146	5. **Do not hide an answer from its initiator:** recipients normally reply and
147	   leave closure to the initiator. For a human-started thread, answer it but leave
148	   it open for the human to consume/archive unless the human explicitly delegates
149	   closure. Use `complete` instead of `archive` only when the concluded thread is
150	   intentionally meant to remain visible in the resolved working record.
151	6. **End-of-session sweep:** before the final report, inspect open conversations
152	   in which your task is `started_by`. Archive every resolved one and state a real
153	   blocker on any that must remain open. An accumulation of open conversations is
154	   unfinished coordination, not harmless history.
155	
156	- `horizon inbox comment <id> --body "..."` — progress note on an item (record
157	  what you did; not to ask the human for clarification). Do not write your name
158	  into the comment body; the author is set automatically. Drop a comment at each **key advance**
159	  while you work an item (a milestone reached, a route ruled out, a blocker hit),
160	  not only at the end — these comments are the item's visible progress trail.
161	- `horizon inbox dm task:<id> [task:<id> ...] --body "Topic\n\nOpening message"`
162	  — start a one-to-one or group conversation. Use `horizon ps` to discover live
163	  teams. Use it only after the lifecycle search above. The sender remains a
164	  participant and owns closure; every reply makes the thread unread for the other
165	  participants. Humans read and reply from the live dashboard.
166	- **Write comments as mathematics, for a human.** State the key step that
167	  succeeded in human-readable mathematical language (LaTeX for formulas), naming
168	  the result and the idea — e.g. "Proved $H^i(X,\mathcal{F})=0$ for $i>\dim X$ by
169	  reducing to the affine case via Čech cohomology." Mention Lean declaration
170	  names and file paths only as supporting detail; the substance is the maths, not
171	  a code changelog. This applies to comments on **roadmap items and tasks** too:
172	  when a key step lands, record it there in the same mathematical, legible style.
173	- `horizon inbox archive <id>` — soft-delete: keep the item for the record but
174	  hide it from the dashboard by default. Use for stale, superseded, consumed, or
175	  no-longer-key context. Keeping the inbox tidy this way is your job (or the
176	  janitor subagent's) — prune memory/info so they remain small.
177	  For a conversation you initiated, this is the normal "discussion finished"
178	  operation after its answer/conclusion has been consumed.
179	- `horizon inbox complete <id>` — mark an item resolved only when it records work
180	  you genuinely concluded and want to keep visible outside the archive. Before
181	  completing, add a short **conclusion comment**: first the mathematical
182	  conclusion (what was proved/established, in words + LaTeX), then concise
183	  metadata (runs, approximate LOC, files/declarations involved). A reader should
184	  grasp the result and how it was concluded without opening the logs.
185	- `horizon inbox add --body "Short title\n\nDescription with details and next action." [--to R] [--project P] [--persistent|--temporary] [--agent <name> if a subagent]`
186	  — open a new item.
187	  - `--to` is the recipient: `horizon`, `human`, `project:<name>`, or a direct
188	    message to another team `task:<id>` / `run:<id>`.
189	    Use `--to project:<name>` to message another project (e.g. "I rewrote your
190	    `foo` declaration more cleanly, you may want it"); use `--to task:<id>` to
191	    message a specific running team.
192	  - `--owner <task-id>` / `--mine` keeps the item in one team's inbox instead of
193	    the shared default.
194	  - `--project` says what the item is ABOUT (its subject).
195	  - `--persistent` / `--temporary` just prepend a `[persistent]` / `[temporary]`
196	    tag to the body.
197	  - `--pending` labels the item `not-ready` instead of the default `agent-ready`,
198	    so it stays invisible to agents until a human releases it.
199	- `horizon inbox add --kind memory --to horizon --body "Short memory title\n\nDurable fact, convention, or dead end."` — record a durable
200	  note / dead end. Memory lives in the inbox, so it is rendered in the "Memory"
201	  section and a human can prune it like any other item.
202	- `horizon inbox protect --body "..." [--project P] [--file F] [--declaration D] [--blueprint-node N]`
203	  — add a semantic standing constraint the Horizon agent must respect (a soft freeze),
204	  e.g. "do not change the signature of `Foo.bar`". These render as a
205	  "Protected" section; honour them, including semantic ones. For a target that
206	  must be mechanically blocked before dispatch, the user uses the config-backed
207	  `horizon freeze add <file|declaration|blueprint-node> <target>` command instead.
208	
209	Reading convention: an item tagged `[persistent]` is a standing rule — respect
210	it every round and keep it open while relevant. `[temporary]` (or untagged) is
211	one-shot — archive it once consumed. Items in the "Protected" section are never
212	modified.

6	import AlgebraicJacobian.Picard.DivisorFamilyAffPerPiece
7	
8	/-!
9	# cert-collapse on the widened cover: the diagonal is degenerate, and what that forces
10	
11	Roadmap leaf `AJCR.w4-rep.datum.dat-d.ddr.certificate.cert-collapse`, restated over
12	`AffCoverData`.  The leaf's ORIGINAL claim — that (c2)/(c3)/(c4) are FREE for a
13	swallow-or-miss adaptation — was **refuted** by work-reviewer at I-0340 and must not be
14	re-derived.  This file lands the structural fact behind the refutation, and the corrected
15	positive statement, on the widened structure.
16	
17	## The refutation, now kernel-checked rather than argued
18	
19	`toOvlLeft i i = toOvlRight i i` holds by `rfl`: at `pieces i ⊓ pieces i` proof irrelevance
20	makes `inf_le_left` and `inf_le_right` the same proof, so the two arrows are literally the
21	same map (`toOvl_diag_eq`).  Hence **every diagonal component of `deltaLeft - deltaRight`
22	is identically zero** (`deltaSub_apply_diag`), for every adaptation over every cover.
23	
24	The consequence, which is why "free" is false: the cokernel of the difference arrow always
25	retains the diagonal factor `∏_i ovlColength i i`, so clause (c4) forces flatness of those
26	overlap colengths — it can never be discharged by a structural observation about which
27	pieces meet the support.  `away-kerspan` therefore stays blocked rather than rejected.
28	
29	## The corrected positive statement
30	
31	What survives is a REDUCTION, not a retirement: on a swallow-or-miss adaptation every piece
32	either swallows the support or misses it, and a missing piece contributes a VANISHING
33	colength and vanishing overlap colengths (`subsingleton_colength_of_disjoint_supportLocus`,
34	`subsingleton_ovlColength_of_disjoint`).  A subsingleton module is free of rank zero, hence
35	flat and projective, so all the missing-piece factors are free of content and only the
36	swallowing pieces carry the certificate — at most one per connected component of the
37	support, rather than one per chart.
38	
39	## Main declarations
40	
41	* `AffAdaptation.toOvl_diag_eq` — the two overlap arrows agree on the diagonal, by `rfl`.
42	* `AffAdaptation.deltaSub_apply_diag` — every diagonal component of the difference vanishes.
43	* `AffAdaptation.subsingleton_ovlColength_of_disjoint` — a piece missing the support kills
44	  its overlap colengths too.
45	* `AffAdaptation.flat_colength_of_disjoint_supportLocus`,
46	  `projective_colength_of_disjoint_supportLocus` — the missing-piece clauses (c1), free of
47	  any fibrewise-regularity input.
48	-/
49	
50	set_option autoImplicit false
51	set_option backward.isDefEq.respectTransparency false
52	set_option maxSynthPendingDepth 3
53	
54	universe u
55	
56	open CategoryTheory TopologicalSpace Opposite
57	
58	namespace AlgebraicGeometry
59	
60	attribute [local instance] Scheme.overModule Scheme.overSectionsAlgebra
61	
62	namespace AffAdaptation
63	
64	variable {k : Type u} [Field k] {C : Over (Spec (.of k))}
65	variable {R : Type u} [CommRing R] [Algebra k R]
66	variable {D : AffCoverData C R} {d : (relCurve C R).LocalEquations}
67	variable (A : AffAdaptation D d)
68	
69	/-! ## The diagonal degeneracy (the I-0340 refutation, kernel-checked) -/
70	
71	/-- **The two overlap arrows agree on the diagonal.**  At `pieces i ⊓ pieces i` the
72	restrictions `inf_le_left` and `inf_le_right` are the same proof of the same inequality, and
73	`ovlIdeal i i` is symmetric in its two generators, so the two lifts are the same map — by
74	`rfl`, no transport.
75	
76	This is the whole content of the I-0340 refutation of this leaf's original claim. -/
77	lemma toOvl_diag_eq (i : D.index) : A.toOvlLeft i i = A.toOvlRight i i := rfl
78	
79	/-- **Every diagonal component of the difference arrow vanishes identically**, for every
80	adaptation over every cover.  Therefore `coker (deltaLeft - deltaRight)` always retains
81	`∏_i ovlColength i i` as a direct factor, and clause (c4) can never be free: it forces
82	flatness of the diagonal overlap colengths.  This is why `cert-collapse` is a reduction and
83	`away-kerspan` stays blocked. -/
84	lemma deltaSub_apply_diag (s : A.chartProd) (i : D.index) :
85	    (A.deltaLeft - A.deltaRight) s (i, i) = 0 := by
86	  simp only [LinearMap.sub_apply, deltaLeft, deltaRight, LinearMap.pi_apply,
87	    LinearMap.coe_comp, Function.comp_apply, LinearMap.proj_apply,
88	    AlgHom.toLinearMap_apply, Pi.sub_apply]
89	  rw [show A.toOvlLeft i i = A.toOvlRight i i from A.toOvl_diag_eq i, sub_self]
90	
91	/-! ## Missing pieces contribute nothing -/
92	
93	/-- **A piece missing the support kills its overlap colengths too**: its restricted equation
94	is a unit on the overlap, and the overlap ideal contains it. -/
95	lemma subsingleton_ovlColength_of_disjoint (i j : D.index)
96	    (hdisj : ∀ z : relCurve C R, z ∈ D.pieces i ⊓ D.pieces j → z ∉ d.supportLocus) :
97	    Subsingleton (A.ovlColength i j) := by
98	  have hunit : IsUnit (relResAlgHom C R
99	      (inf_le_left : D.pieces i ⊓ D.pieces j ≤ D.pieces i) (A.eqn i)) := by
100	    rw [relResAlgHom_apply]
101	    apply (relCurve C R).toRingedSpace.isUnit_of_isUnit_germ
102	    intro z hz
103	    rw [(relCurve C R).presheaf.germ_res_apply]
104	    have hU : z ∈ d.unitLocus := not_not.mp (hdisj z hz)
105	    exact (A.isUnit_germ_eqn_iff i (inf_le_left (α := (relCurve C R).Opens) hz)).mpr
106	      ((d.mem_unitLocus_iff_isUnit_germ (d.cover.mem_opens z)).mp hU)
107	  exact Ideal.Quotient.subsingleton_iff.mpr
108	    (Ideal.eq_top_of_isUnit_mem _ (Ideal.subset_span (Set.mem_insert _ _)) hunit)
109	
110	/-- A missing piece's colength module is flat — it is subsingleton, hence free of rank
111	zero.  No fibrewise-regularity input, no Noetherian hypothesis. -/
112	lemma flat_colength_of_disjoint_supportLocus (j : D.index)
113	    (hdisj : ∀ z : relCurve C R, z ∈ D.pieces j → z ∉ d.supportLocus) :
114	    Module.Flat R (A.colength j) := by
115	  haveI := A.subsingleton_colength_of_disjoint_supportLocus j hdisj
116	  haveI : Module.Free R (A.colength j) := Module.Free.of_subsingleton R (A.colength j)
117	  exact Module.Flat.of_free
118	
119	/-- A missing piece's colength module is projective, for the same reason. -/
120	lemma projective_colength_of_disjoint_supportLocus (j : D.index)
121	    (hdisj : ∀ z : relCurve C R, z ∈ D.pieces j → z ∉ d.supportLocus) :
122	    Module.Projective R (A.colength j) := by
123	  haveI := A.subsingleton_colength_of_disjoint_supportLocus j hdisj
124	  haveI : Module.Free R (A.colength j) := Module.Free.of_subsingleton R (A.colength j)
125	  exact Module.Projective.of_free

**THE `PicScheme.degree` "STATEMENT-LEVEL DEFECT" IS OVERSTATED (commit f820eff22, `Picard/IdentityComponent.lean:1454-1465`). Two of its three sentences are refuted by a compiled probe.**

The docstring asserts: (1) an arbitrary `l : Spec k ⟶ (PicScheme C).left` need not be a section, so (2) "representability says nothing about it", and (3) "a total function of that type cannot be built from the Picard functor at all; it would have to invent a value off the sections".

(1) is correct. (2) and (3) are false.

(2) Representability DOES apply to every such `l`: `l` is a morphism in `Over (Spec k)` out of the test object `Over.mk (l ≫ (PicScheme C).hom)` — the twisted `Spec k` — and `Over.homMk l rfl` typechecks with `rfl` as the commuting proof. Verified sorry-free:
```
noncomputable def classOfAnyMorphism [HasPicScheme C] (l : Spec (.of k) ⟶ (PicScheme C).left) :
    (PicSharp.relPresheaf C).obj (Opposite.op (Over.mk (l ≫ (PicScheme C).hom))) :=
  (PicScheme.representable C).homEquiv (Over.homMk l rfl)
-- axioms: [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]
```
So `classOfSection`'s restriction to sections is a choice of test object (the trivial one), not a limitation of representability.

import AlgebraicJacobian.Picard.DivisorFamilyAffSwallow
import AlgebraicJacobian.Algebra.PiLocalization

/-!
# The glued clauses on a straddling cover: (c2)/(c3)/(c4) REDUCE to (c1)

The corrected cert-collapse claim (roadmap `...certificate.cert-collapse`, as amended after
the I-0340 refutation), carried out on the widened cover.

## What was refuted and what survives

The refuted claim was that (c2)/(c3)/(c4) are FREE for a swallow-or-miss adaptation.  They are
not, and `DivisorFamilyAffCollapse.lean` kernel-checks why: `toOvlLeft i i = toOvlRight i i`
by `rfl`, so every diagonal component of `deltaLeft - deltaRight` vanishes for EVERY
adaptation, and the diagonal factor always survives in the cokernel.  Clause (c4) therefore
always implies flatness of the diagonal overlap colengths — no structural observation about
which pieces meet the support can remove that.

What survives is the REDUCTION the amended node states: on a cover with a straddling piece,
(c2)/(c3)/(c4) follow from (c1)-projectivity alone.  This file proves it.

## The mechanism, and it is sharper than the node's account

With a straddling piece `j₀`, every OTHER piece misses the support, so
`subsingleton_ovlColength_of_disjoint` kills every overlap colength that involves an index
`≠ j₀` — in particular every OFF-DIAGONAL one, since a pair `(i, j)` with `i ≠ j` has at least
one entry `≠ j₀`.  Combined with the vanishing diagonal, `deltaLeft - deltaRight` is the ZERO
map (`deltaSub_eq_zero_of_swallowedBy`).  Hence:

* `gluedSubmodule = ⊤`, so `Glued ≃ chartProd` — (c2) becomes a statement about the product of
  the piece colengths, of which all but one are subsingleton;
* `chartProd ⧸ gluedSubmodule` is subsingleton, so (c3) is free — and this IS free, with no
  input, which is the one part of the original claim that was right;
* `range (deltaLeft - deltaRight) = ⊥`, so the (c4) cokernel is `ovlProd` itself, whose
  factors are the overlap colengths: all subsingleton except `ovlColength j₀ j₀`.  So (c4)
  reduces to flatness of THAT ONE module — exactly the residue the refutation predicted, now
  isolated to a single index instead of a whole cover.

## Main declarations

* `AffAdaptation.deltaSub_eq_zero_of_swallowedBy` — the difference arrow vanishes identically.
* `AffAdaptation.gluedSubmodule_eq_top_of_swallowedBy` — the equalizer is everything.
* `AffAdaptation.gluedEquivChartProd_of_swallowedBy` — hence `Glued ≃ₗ chartProd`.
* `AffAdaptation.flat_coker_incl_of_swallowedBy` — clause (c3), unconditionally free.
* `AffAdaptation.flat_coker_diff_of_swallowedBy` — clause (c4) from flatness of the single
  diagonal overlap colength at the straddling piece.
-/

set_option autoImplicit false
set_option backward.isDefEq.respectTransparency false
set_option maxSynthPendingDepth 3

universe u

open CategoryTheory TopologicalSpace Opposite

namespace AlgebraicGeometry

attribute [local instance] Scheme.overModule Scheme.overSectionsAlgebra

namespace AffAdaptation

variable {k : Type u} [Field k] {C : Over (Spec (.of k))}
variable {R : Type u} [CommRing R] [Algebra k R]
variable {D : AffCoverData C R} {d : (relCurve C R).LocalEquations}
variable (A : AffAdaptation D d)

/-! ## Every overlap colength off the straddling diagonal vanishes -/

/-- **An overlap involving a missing piece has vanishing colength.**  `SwallowedBy` says every
piece other than `j₀` is disjoint from the support, and an overlap is contained in each of its
two pieces, so it too misses the support. -/
lemma subsingleton_ovlColength_of_swallowedBy {j₀ : D.index}
    (hmiss : ∀ j : D.index, j ≠ j₀ →
      Disjoint d.supportLocus (D.pieces j : Set (relCurve C R)))
    (i j : D.index) (h : i ≠ j₀ ∨ j ≠ j₀) :
    Subsingleton (A.ovlColength i j) := by
  refine A.subsingleton_ovlColength_of_disjoint i j fun z hz hsupp => ?_
  rcases h with hi | hj
  · exact (Set.disjoint_left.mp (hmiss i hi)) hsupp hz.1
  · exact (Set.disjoint_left.mp (hmiss j hj)) hsupp hz.2

/-- **The difference arrow is identically zero on a straddling cover.**  On the diagonal it
vanishes for every adaptation whatsoever (`deltaSub_apply_diag`, the I-0340 fact); off the
diagonal the target is subsingleton, because a pair `(i, j)` with `i ≠ j` has at least one
entry different from the straddling index. -/
theorem deltaSub_eq_zero_of_swallowedBy (h : D.SwallowedBy d) :
    A.deltaLeft - A.deltaRight = 0 := by
  obtain ⟨j₀, _, hmiss⟩ := h
  refine LinearMap.ext fun s => funext fun p => ?_
  by_cases hp : p.1 = p.2
  · -- diagonal: zero for every adaptation, by proof irrelevance on `inf_le_left/right`
    obtain ⟨i, j⟩ := p
    cases hp
    exact A.deltaSub_apply_diag s i
  · -- off-diagonal: at least one index misses the support, so the target is trivial
    haveI : Subsingleton (A.ovlColength p.1 p.2) := by
      by_cases h1 : p.1 = j₀
      · exact A.subsingleton_ovlColength_of_swallowedBy hmiss p.1 p.2
          (Or.inr fun h2 => hp (h1.trans h2.symm))
      · exact A.subsingleton_ovlColength_of_swallowedBy hmiss p.1 p.2 (Or.inl h1)
    exact Subsingleton.elim _ _

/-! ## The consequences for (c2)/(c3)/(c4) -/

/-- **The equalizer is everything**: with the difference arrow zero, every section glues. -/
theorem gluedSubmodule_eq_top_of_swallowedBy (h : D.SwallowedBy d) :
    A.gluedSubmodule = ⊤ := by
  rw [gluedSubmodule, A.deltaSub_eq_zero_of_swallowedBy h]
  exact LinearMap.ker_zero

/-- **Hence the glued module is the whole product of piece colengths.**  This is what makes
(c2) a statement about the piece colengths — of which, on a straddling cover, all but the
swallowing one are subsingleton. -/
noncomputable def gluedEquivChartProd_of_swallowedBy (h : D.SwallowedBy d) :
    A.Glued ≃ₗ[R] A.chartProd :=
  (LinearEquiv.ofEq _ _ (A.gluedSubmodule_eq_top_of_swallowedBy h)).trans
    Submodule.topEquiv

/-- **Clause (c3) is free on a straddling cover** — no fibrewise input, no Noetherian
hypothesis, nothing.  The inclusion `W(d) ↪ ∏ colength` is onto, so its cokernel is trivial.
This is the one part of this leaf's refuted original claim that was correct. -/
theorem flat_coker_incl_of_swallowedBy (h : D.SwallowedBy d) :
    Module.Flat R (A.chartProd ⧸ A.gluedSubmodule) := by
  haveI : Subsingleton (A.chartProd ⧸ A.gluedSubmodule) := by
    rw [A.gluedSubmodule_eq_top_of_swallowedBy h]; infer_instance
  haveI : Module.Free R (A.chartProd ⧸ A.gluedSubmodule) :=
    Module.Free.of_subsingleton R _
  exact Module.Flat.of_free

/-- **Clause (c2)-finiteness reduces to the piece colengths.** -/
theorem finite_glued_of_swallowedBy [Fintype D.index] (h : D.SwallowedBy d)
    (hfin : ∀ j, Module.Finite R (A.colength j)) :
    Module.Finite R A.Glued := by
  haveI := hfin
  haveI : Module.Finite R A.chartProd := Module.Finite.pi
  exact Module.Finite.equiv (A.gluedEquivChartProd_of_swallowedBy h).symm

/-- **Clause (c2)-projectivity reduces to the piece colengths.** -/
theorem projective_glued_of_swallowedBy (h : D.SwallowedBy d)
    (hproj : ∀ j, Module.Projective R (A.colength j)) :
    Module.Projective R A.Glued := by
  haveI := hproj
  haveI : Module.Projective R A.chartProd := Module.Projective.pi
  exact Module.Projective.of_equiv (A.gluedEquivChartProd_of_swallowedBy h).symm

/-- **Clause (c4) reduces to flatness of the piece colengths alone.**  The difference arrow is
zero, so its cokernel is `ovlProd` itself; every off-`j₀` factor is subsingleton, and the
surviving factor `ovlColength j₀ j₀` is the diagonal overlap of the straddling piece, whose
flatness is what the refutation identified as unavoidable.  It is supplied here as `hdiag`,
one module rather than a whole cover — which is precisely the reduction the amended
cert-collapse node claims. -/
theorem flat_coker_diff_of_swallowedBy [Fintype D.index] (h : D.SwallowedBy d)
    (hdiag : ∀ i j : D.index, Module.Flat R (A.ovlColength i j)) :
    Module.Flat R (A.ovlProd ⧸ LinearMap.range (A.deltaLeft - A.deltaRight)) := by
  haveI : ∀ p : D.index × D.index, Module.Flat R (A.ovlColength p.1 p.2) :=
    fun p => hdiag p.1 p.2
  haveI : Module.Flat R A.ovlProd := Module.Flat.pi_of_finite
  have hrange : LinearMap.range (A.deltaLeft - A.deltaRight) = ⊥ := by
    rw [A.deltaSub_eq_zero_of_swallowedBy h]; exact LinearMap.range_zero
  rw [hrange]
  exact Module.Flat.of_linearEquiv (Submodule.quotEquivOfEqBot ⊥ rfl)

end AffAdaptation
